Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the UniBank Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, ladies and gentlemen, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to review UniBank's results for the Q3 2024. With me this morning are David Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Reynolds, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Risk Officer; and Robert Hayes, Chief Credit Officer.

Before we begin, let me remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a discussion of these factors.

I will now turn the call over to David Thompson.

David Thompson:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. UniBank delivered strong performance in the Q3, driven by our commitment to customer service and operational excellence.

Our key priorities for this year remain focused on:
1. Growing our core businesses
2. Investing in technology and innovation
3. Managing risk effectively
4. Optimizing our capital allocation
5. Enhancing our employee engagement.

Now, I'd like to provide some highlights on key areas. Starting with provision for credit losses, we recorded $525 million in Q3, reflecting disciplined CECL application amid mixed macro signals, with our allowance at $12.4 billion or 1.18% of loans. On capital return plans, our CET1 stands robust at 12.8%, supporting a 10% dividend hike to $0.48 quarterly and $2.8 billion in YTD buybacks. Regarding the macroeconomic outlook, we see a bifurcated global recovery with U.S. GDP at 2.4% and opportunities in APAC offsetting CRE pressures. Operating expenses totaled $2.48 billion, up modestly with tech investments driving efficiency to 58.2%. Finally, our guidance assumes a soft landing, full-year adjusted EPS of $5.75 to $6.00, and ROTCE in the mid-teens.

I will now turn the call over to Michael Reynolds to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you, David, and good morning. UniBank reported net income of $1.2 billion for the Q3, or $1.85 per share. Our results reflect strong revenue growth, disciplined expense management, and a healthy credit environment.

Net interest income increased 8% year-over-year due to loan growth and improved net interest margin. Non-interest income was up 10% year-over-year. Key performance indicators include ROTCE of 14.2% and an efficiency ratio of 58.2%. We are confident in our ability to achieve our financial goals for the year.

Let me now dive deeper into our provision for credit losses, or PCL, which totaled $525 million in Q3 2024, a 12% increase from $470 million in Q2 but stable year-over-year. This outcome demonstrates our rigorous adherence to the CECL framework under ASC 326, navigating a varied economic landscape where commercial segments face headwinds balanced by strength in consumer and mortgage areas. Our overall allowance for credit losses reached $12.4 billion, equivalent to 1.18% of total loans held for investment—up 5 basis points sequentially and exceeding our through-the-cycle norm of 1.05%. Coverage is solid at 320% of annualized net charge-offs and 4.2 times criticized and classified loans.

For context, our approach involves estimating lifetime expected losses on a pooled basis for our $1.05 trillion loan book using a discounted cash flow model built on probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD), and exposure at default (EAD). PDs come from logistic regression models using over 20 years of internal data, supplemented by Moody's and S&P benchmarks. LGDs account for collateral values, historical recovery patterns, and downturn adjustments—averaging 42% for unsecured consumer loans and 25% for CRE first liens. EAD factors in prepayments, draws on commitments, and revolver trends.

Our forward-looking adjustments are key: we simulate 12 macro scenarios through our Economic Scenario Generator, validated against Fed SR 15-19 and CCAR standards, ranging from baseline 2.1% U.S. GDP to severe -3.5% contraction mimicking 2008-09. Forecasts pull from Philadelphia Fed Survey, IMF outlooks, and internal analysis, with a 45% weighting on mildly adverse cases this quarter—up from 35% in Q2 amid cooling employment.

The quarter's provision was influenced by portfolio shifts, credit migrations, and macro factors. Commercial real estate accounted for 55% or $290 million of the build, with our $180 billion CRE portfolio—20% office, 30% multifamily, 25% industrial—showing PDs up 15 basis points to 1.85%, hit by 18-20% office vacancies in NYC and San Francisco per CoStar, exacerbated by remote work and refinancing into 5.3% 10-year Treasuries, dropping DSCRs under 1.2x for 12% of office loans. Industrial CRE stayed firm at 0.9% PD, aided by e-commerce similar to Prologis. Consumer lending contributed only 20%, with $120 billion auto loans at 0.65% 30+ day delinquencies due to firm used-car prices (Manheim up 2% QoQ) and super-prime focus (FICO >740); cards saw delinquencies rise 25 basis points to 2.1%, matching Capital One, but charge-offs at 3.8% annualized. Corporate and middle-market C&I ($250 billion) added $140 million, pressured by energy and retail with LGDs up 5 basis points to 38% amid sub-$70 WTI oil.

Credit trends included an 8% QoQ rise in criticized loans to $15.2 billion (1.4% of loans), mainly CRE special mentions; net charge-offs to 0.52% annualized from 0.45%, in non-prime cards and small business; early delinquencies up 18 basis points to 1.35%, hinting at C&I weakness post-SVB.

Macro dynamics featured U.S. consumer resilience (4.2% unemployment per BLS) bolstering $300 billion mortgages (0.4% PD), but we added 10 basis point overlays for recession risks. Our $150 billion European book via UK plc contributed $60 million from commercial property writedowns like Barclays', with retail DSCR compression; Asia-Pacific ($80 billion ex-China) at 0.7% PD benefited from Singapore tech growth, after trimming 5% China exposure.

On enhancements, we launched Phase 2 of our AI/ML PD models using XGBoost and neural nets on 50 million data points, improving backtest accuracy 12% versus 2023 bank failures. Alternative data from Zellic for CRE cash flows and Plaid for consumer cut uncertainty 15%; climate overlays per NGFS raised coastal mortgage LGDs 3 basis points. Model Risk Management validated IFRS 9 alignment for Europe.

Proactively, we tightened CRE to 1.3x min DSCR and 65% LTV, syndicating $2.5 billion or 10% office exposure; shifting to ABL and equipment finance for 15% growth by 2025 like Wells Fargo; consumer growing 7% via digital platforms. Q4 PCL outlook: $480-530 million barring Fed shifts; higher if unemployment >4.5% or office caps >8%, releases possible on stabilization. CET1 at 11.8% buffers GSIB needs.

Next, let's discuss operating expenses, or non-interest expenses, which totaled $2.48 billion in Q3, rising 4.2% year-over-year but flat sequentially. This yielded an efficiency ratio of 58.2%, improved 110 basis points YoY and peer-competitive per S&P Global.

By category: Compensation and benefits, 42% of OpEx at $1.04 billion, grew just 1.8% YoY versus 4-5% wage inflation, with global FTEs at 92,000 down 2% post-2022 restructuring via automation and attrition. Incentives moderated on ROTCE and CET1 metrics. Talent competition in digital and quant risk drove 10-15% premiums for AI experts like at JPM and Goldman; countered by Coursera partnerships and fintech training, holding benefits to 2.1% growth despite U.S. healthcare rises.

Technology and data jumped 18% YoY to $580 million (23% of OpEx), focused on ROI: AWS/Azure cloud at 65% complete slashed data center costs 25%, enabling real-time consumer analytics. GenAI chatbots cut call times 30% and deflected 15% inquiries like Wells Fargo; RL fraud models reduced false positives 22%, saving $45 million yearly. Cybersecurity $120 million for zero-trust amid ransomware, ahead of Basel III ops resilience. APAC up 25% for WeChat integration, volumes +40% vs. Grab/Ant; EMEA flat on mainframe cuts.

Professional fees fell 8% to $320 million via 20% outsourcing to Infosys/Accenture for 15-20% savings; U.S. Dodd-Frank/LIBOR $50 million, EMEA DORA/SFDR up 12% to $180 million. Occupancy/equipment +3% to $210 million on 45 branch closures but hybrid workspaces; marketing +5% to $110 million on digital acquisition (3x ROI).

Geographically: U.S. (55%) +3% offset by productivity post-Capital One stack, FDIC premiums to 7 bps; EMEA (25%) +7% on Brexit/MiFID but fee offsets better than HSBC; APAC +2% despite 12% revenue growth via Alipay.

Forward, Q4 OpEx $2.5-2.55 billion (4-5% YoY), tech moderating to 12-15%; efficiency to 57%. Structural 2-3% CAGR via ZBB, $150 million FinTechOne synergies, AI procure-to-pay.

Turning to our macroeconomic outlook and its impacts, our diversified operations across commercial banking, consumer, wealth, and markets equip us well, with CET1 at 12.8% buffering Basel IV. Global GDP at 3.1% for 2024 per internal/IMF models, down from 3.3% on supply/geopolitics; inflation sticky—U.S. core PCE 2.6%, Euro HICP 2.4%, India 4.8%. Fed terminal 4.75-5.00% with Q4 cuts; ECB at 3.25% post-75 bps; PBOC stimulus for China 4.7% GDP.

U.S.: 2.4% GDP 2024 to 2.6% 2025 on consumer (sales +2.9%) and AI capex; unemployment 4.1% keeps card delinquencies 2.8% vs. 3.5% average. CRE vigilance on $45 billion (85% office), caps to 7.2%; reserved $150 million Q2, NPL 1.2%. NIM 3.45% +12 bps QoQ on 65/35 fixed-floating, deposit beta 45%, high-yield savings 4.2%; to 3.60% year-end (+$400 million NII). Loans +5.2% YoY, C&I 7% on semis/renewables.

Europe (£28 billion London/Frankfurt): 0.9% GDP on German slowdown; ECB aids €15 billion mortgages at 2.8% funding; cap markets fees +14% on €200 billion M&A, AI FX hedging cuts slippage 15 bps, trading +8%.

APAC (18% assets): 5.2% GDP, ASEAN trade finance +22%; China derisked 12% post-property, pivot to $2.5 billion green bonds; India +15% via HDFC/UPI.

Risks: 35% recession odds on nowcast; NCOs 45 bps pristine. Opportunities: $18 billion deposits on 4.5% CDs. Initiatives: GenAI risk scoring cuts approvals 40%, autos +18% to $12 billion; $50 billion sustainable deposits for 15% ROE green premiums; $1.2 billion buybacks. NII +6-8%, EPS $4.85-4.95, ROTE 11.5%.

On capital returns, strategy and outlook form a pillar of value creation with our strong balance sheet. CET1 12.8% standardized >11.5% target and 10.5% reg min incl. G-SIB; Tier 1 leverage 6.2%, SLR 5.8%; CCAR passed with 9.2% post-stress; organic gen 140 bps on 15% ROE.

Dividends: Board hiked 10% to $0.48 quarterly ($1.92 ann., 3.1% yield), 14th straight increase, 38% payout vs. 35-45% target. U.S. deposit stabilization +8% NII; Europe hedged euro payouts. 2025 mid-single digit growth if ROTCE >13%, NPL 0.9%.

Share repurchases: $6 billion authorization; $2.8 billion YTD at $62.50 avg. (3.2% yield), 4.2% shares retired (+2 cents EPS). 10b5-1 60%, discretionary on volatility; $3.2 billion remains, $1 billion Q4. Gated by CET1 >11.5%, growth ($1.2 billion digital/AI/Palantir/AWS), M&A ($450 million Midwest bank).

Regional: U.S. (65% RWA) boosted by IB fees +22%; APAC (15%) tempered on trade finance; LatAm (10%) +12% local dividends on Selic.

Outlook: $10-12 billion returns 12-18 months (60/40 div/buyback), 9-11% yield, +$1.20 EPS; upside on cuts, downside prioritizes CET1 to 13.5%. Basel IV for 50 bps RWA relief; ESG $500 million green deposits.

Finally, on key assumptions for full-year 2024 guidance—adjusted EPS $5.75-$6.00 (+8-12%), revenue +6-9%, ROTCE 14-15% building on Q3 11% revenue (+4.2% loans, NII +320 bps YoY).

Macro/rates: U.S. soft landing 2.0-2.5% GDP, unemployment 4.1-4.3%, PCE 2.5-2.8%, two 25 bps Fed cuts to 4.50-4.75%, NIM 3.45-3.55%. Europe ECB peak 4.25%, 1.0-1.5% GDP; APAC 4.5-5.5%, 10-12% loans. Oil shock stress-tested.

Balance sheet: Loans +4-5% (C&I 5-7%, consumer 6%, mortgages $25-30 billion); deposits +3-4% (core 72%, beta 0.35); wholesale $20-25 billion SOFR+25.

Credit: NCOs 55-65 bps, consumer delinq 1.8%, commercial criticized <2.5%, office 3% loans Class A LTV<55%; prov $1.8-2.0 billion, coverage 1.10-1.15%; 15% downturn prob.

Non-interest: Fees +7-10% (IB +15% $1.2 billion, cards +9% 5 million wallets, trading $800-900 million, $150 million BaaS).

Expenses: +4-5% to $11.2-11.4 billion, jaw 150-200 bps, efficiency 56-58%; $500 million tech (cloud 60%, Palantir AI $50 million save, RPA 30%); 50 U.S. branches close, Europe rationalization.

Capital: CET1 11.8-12.2% >10.5%; $4.5 billion returns ($2.0 billion buybacks $85-95, $2.5 billion divs); M&A wealth $5-10 billion, digital 20% new accounts.

Dynamic, updated quarterly; resilient to inflation/cyber via $1.2 billion spend.

Lisa Chen:
Thank you, Michael. As Chief Risk Officer, I would like to briefly discuss our risk management framework. We continue to prioritize proactive risk identification and mitigation. Our key focus areas include credit migration in CRE and operational resilience amid cyber threats. We remain vigilant in monitoring emerging risks like geopolitical tensions and adapting our strategies accordingly.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator:
Ladies and gentlemen, as a reminder, if you'd like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith:
Good morning. Can you provide more detail on your outlook for loan growth and deposit betas?

David Thompson:
Good morning, John. Thanks for the question. Our loan growth guidance of 4-5% for the year, accelerating to 5-6% in Q4, is driven by C&I expansion at 5-7% in renewables and tech middle-market, consumer up 6% with cards revolving balances rising 8% on resilient spending akin to JPMorgan and Capital One trends, and mortgages stabilizing at $25-30 billion on purchase volumes up 15% with housing starts at 1.45 million. Deposits grow 3-4%, anchored by low-cost core at $450 billion with a 0.35 beta—we're managing this through premium CDs at 4.25% APY and relationship incentives, keeping core at 72% of funding. We've seen inflows of $18 billion recently as our products compete well against money markets. This supports NIM expansion to 3.60% by year-end. Happy to follow up offline.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Davis with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Emily Davis:
What are your expectations for net interest margin expansion?

Michael Reynolds:
Thanks, Emily. Our Q3 NIM hit 3.45%, up 12 basis points sequentially, thanks to our 65/35 fixed-to-floating mix and deposit betas compressing to 45% as clients move to our 4.2% high-yield savings. We project 3.60% by year-end under base case with Fed funds at 4.50-4.75% post-two cuts, adding about $400 million annually to NII. This assumes stable loan growth and deposit optimization. Upside from faster cuts boosting demand, but we're hedged against higher-for-longer with swaps. Confident in 6-8% NII growth for the year.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mike Patel with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Mike Patel:
Can you comment on the credit quality of your CRE portfolio?

Robert Hayes:
Good morning, Mike. Our CRE book is $180 billion, with office at 20% or $36 billion, prudently managed—PDs rose 15 basis points to 1.85% on vacancies 18-20% in key cities and refinancing pressures, but we've tightened to 1.3x DSCR min and 65% LTV, syndicating $2.5 billion or 10% office exposure. Criticized loans up but coverage 320% of NCOs; NPLs low at 1.2% overall. Industrial steady at 0.9% PD on e-commerce. De-risking into ABL/equipment for diversification. Q4 stable assuming no cap rate surge beyond 8%. Solid buffer.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn the conference back over to David Thompson for any closing remarks.

David Thompson:
Thank you for your interest in UniBank. We appreciate you joining us today. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
